strengths: Addresses important gap in bilingual fine-grained vision-language understanding, particularly for Chinese which is under-explored
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 diverse tasks on 29 datasets demonstrates broad applicability and consistent improvements
Contributes new Chinese benchmarks (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) that provide valuable evaluation infrastructure for the community

weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: nearly all components (SigLIP 2 backbone, region supervision, CMR loss, sigmoid loss) are adaptations of existing work; TIC loss is straightforward intra-modal contrastive learning

Critical methodological flaw: BoxClass-CN is constructed using FG-CLIP for object detection and similarity filtering, then FG-CLIP 2 is evaluated on this FG-CLIP-constructed dataset, creating circular evaluation bias that disadvantages other methods

Heavy reliance on proprietary in-house datasets (500M Chinese pairs for stage 1, 12M for stage 2) that cannot be shared or validated; total 3.4B image-text pairs significantly exceeds baselines, making it unclear whether improvements come from method or dataset advantages

Insufficient ablation studies: missing ablations on long caption training alone, bilingual vs. monolingual training, two-stage vs. single-stage paradigm, and contribution of individual data sources; loss weights and similarity thresholds appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis

Unfair baseline comparisons: SigLIP 2 shows catastrophic failure on Chinese (4.5% vs 82.4%) with no explanation; comparison with Meta CLIP 2 (true multilingual SOTA) more informative but receives less emphasis

Benchmark construction concerns: LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN use LMM-generated or machine-translated captions without inter-annotator agreement; risk of systematic biases from machine translation and LMM caption artifacts

Poor reproducibility: in-house datasets cannot be validated, massive computational requirements (160×ASCEND 910B + 16×NVIDIA H800) are inaccessible to most researchers, exact LMM caption pipeline not fully specified
No statistical rigor: single runs reported with no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; some improvements marginal (1.5 points on ImageNet-1K)
Gaps in analysis: no computational cost comparison, limited parameter efficiency analysis, no explanation of when/why the method helps across different task types
Limitations discussion (Section 5) is generic and fails to acknowledge key concerns including BoxClass-CN circularity and data advantage implications

Consistent improvements across both languages and model scales, with notably strong gains on fine-grained tasks (FG-OVD hard: 52.3% vs 46.1% for FG-CLIP ViT-B)

weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: TIC loss (Eq. 4) is a straightforward contrastive loss applied to text embeddings with no substantial innovation over existing contrastive learning methods; all other components are borrowed from SigLIP, FG-CLIP, and prior work

Evaluation bias risk: exceptionally strong performance on newly created Chinese datasets (LIT-CN 86.3% I→T ViT-L) may reflect overfitting to LMM generation process rather than genuine capability improvement

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 29 datasets and 8 distinct vision-language tasks with rigorous ablation studies and re-trained baselines for fair comparison

Significant practical contributions including two 12M-scale datasets (FineRegion-CN and region-text pairs) and four new Chinese benchmarks (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) that fill important gaps for bilingual research
Well-engineered two-stage training paradigm that effectively combines global semantic alignment with fine-grained region-level supervision, demonstrating strong empirical results
Thorough implementation documentation and hyperparameter justification (Appendices F-H) supporting reproducibility and methodology transparency
The TIC loss provides a straightforward yet effective approach to text discrimination, with clear benefits demonstrated in ablations (~4.8 points on COCO)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: architecture largely adapted from SigLIP 2, most loss functions borrowed (sigmoid, CMR), and approach primarily represents careful engineering rather than fundamental innovation

Critical design choices lack rigorous justification: similarity threshold (>0.95), top-10 hard negatives, 196-token extension, and loss weight values (λ₁=0.1, λ₂=0.5, λ₃=0.1, λ₄=0.4) chosen empirically without systematic ablations or principled reasoning

Severe reproducibility barriers: requires rare ASCEND 910B NPUs (160×) for Stage 1 and split training across different hardware/data regimes; in-house Chinese dataset (500M pairs) unavailable; code repository link absent from PDF

Potential experimental fairness issues: SigLIP 2 baseline shows anomalously poor Chinese performance (14.8% on DCI-CN), raising questions about baseline compatibility; dataset construction relies heavily on LMM-generated content with acknowledged but unquantified translation quality

Incomplete analysis: no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; missing ablations on TIC hyperparameters (why 0.95 threshold, why top-10 negatives); no error analysis, failure cases, or computational cost discussion; visualization improvements lack quantitative validation

strengths: Comprehensive bilingual evaluation across 29 datasets and 8 tasks demonstrates broad applicability and strong empirical results
Valuable resource contributions: FineRegion-CN (12M Chinese region-text pairs) and new Chinese benchmarks (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) address gaps in bilingual multimodal research
Addresses underexplored problem of bilingual fine-grained vision-language alignment in both English and Chinese
Consistent improvements across diverse tasks including competitive performance with smaller models (ViT-L/16) than stronger baselines (ViT-H/14)
Adequate ablation studies and promised open-source release support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: TIC loss is a straightforward intra-modal contrastive learning approach (Eq. 1) lacking conceptual innovation; LFGT reuses FG-CLIP, LCMR is from prior work, and LFGV is basic region-text matching
Architecture modifications are incremental: extending SigLIP 2 with longer text length, data-adaptive resolution, and self-attention modules are minor tweaks rather than innovations

Unclear attribution of gains: improvements appear driven primarily by large-scale curated bilingual data (1.6B+850M image-text, 12M+12M region-text pairs) rather than methodological advances; critical missing experiment decomposing data vs. method contributions

Weak justification for TIC loss: stated purpose is fine-grained understanding but ablation shows only 0.7-point drop on FG-OVD Hard (main fine-grained benchmark), while LCMR removal causes larger drops (52.3%→50.9%), contradicting the claimed importance

Bilingual claims lack depth: unclear if joint training provides synergistic benefits vs. simply providing more aggregate training data; no controlled experiment comparing same-sized English-only vs. mixed bilingual datasets

Evaluation biases: BoxClass-CN construction uses FG-CLIP-based filtering (similarity > 0.15), potentially favoring FG-CLIP 2; limited quality validation metrics and inter-annotator agreement for new benchmarks

Reproducibility limitations: 500M proprietary in-house Chinese data unavailable; long caption generation process underspecified; Stage 1 uses non-standard hardware (160×ASCEND 910B NPUs); hyperparameter justification lacking
Incremental over FG-CLIP: modest improvements (e.g., FG-OVD Hard +6.2 points for ViT-B) with limited methodological novelty for a '2.0' version; overclaims 'state-of-the-art' for 4-7% improvements
Missing technical analysis: no deep investigation of which specific fine-grained phenomena improve, why TIC is necessary given small ablation impact, or error analysis and failure cases
Data-centric rather than method-centric contribution: strong results driven by large curated datasets and extensive tuning rather than novel techniques, reducing impact for a methods-focused venue

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across 29 datasets and 8 diverse tasks with consistent improvements, demonstrating thorough empirical rigor
Outperforms multilingual SOTA (Meta CLIP 2) with 43% smaller model (1.0B vs 1.8B params), suggesting effective method design or data utilization
Valuable dataset contributions: FineRegion-CN (12M region-text pairs) and new Chinese multimodal benchmarks (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) address gaps in bilingual fine-grained resources
Well-motivated two-stage training framework combining global alignment with fine-grained objectives; clear presentation with good organization and implementation details
Demonstrates mutual benefit between English and Chinese (Table C: bilingual improves both languages), supporting the bilingual approach
Strong results on challenging fine-grained understanding tasks (FG-OVD Hard: 52.3% vs FG-CLIP 46.1%), indicating genuine improvements in fine-grained discrimination
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: TIC loss (Eq. 1) is straightforward application of contrastive learning with hard negative mining; CMR loss directly from prior work with minor modifications; overall contribution is primarily engineering/integration rather than fundamental innovation

Insufficient justification for design choices: no sensitivity analysis for 0.95 similarity threshold in TIC, unclear why top-10 hard negatives, loss weight selection through sequential tuning may not find global optimum, data-adaptive resolution not empirically validated

Dataset quality concerns: long captions generated by single LMM introduces systematic bias; hard negatives synthetically perturbed rather than naturally occurring; BoxClass-CN construction uses FG-CLIP for filtering (circular dependency); limited quality control documentation and no inter-annotator agreement for translations

Limited bilingual analysis: no mechanistic explanation of why bilingual helps both languages; no cross-lingual transfer analysis, error analysis, or investigation of language-specific challenges; improvements could stem from data diversity rather than architectural design

Missing critical ablations: no validation of data-adaptive resolution effectiveness, no isolated analysis of long-caption augmentation, limited exploration of alternative two-stage designs, CMR loss shows modest benefit (50.9% vs 52.3%) questioning its necessity

No statistical significance testing despite single runs; no error bars or confidence intervals; significant error analysis absent (no failure cases, no domain breakdown); no computational cost analysis or efficiency discussion
